intro: A repeated B♭ sounds through changing chords and widely spaced melodic fragments. This movement changes pianist: OE1FEU’s own recording on a Bechstein D 282 in Vienna replaces Andriy Makarevych, who plays Ondine and Scarbo in this assembled set.
question: Can an unchanging note make the harmony around it sound more unstable?

sections.label: Bell and first shadows
sections.mNote: repeated B♭ against changing lower chords

sections.label: Widened chordal colour
sections.mNote: the bell persists within thicker sonorities

sections.label: An exposed middle distance
sections.mNote: reduced weight leaves more space around the bell

sections.label: Renewed chordal weight
sections.mNote: harmonic layers thicken without changing the pulse

sections.label: The bell left behind
sections.mNote: chords retreat while the repeated note remains

cues.title: Keep one note in view
cues.text: Find the repeated B♭ and keep following it through the movement. Ravel does not use it as a signal for each new phrase: it continues while chords and melodic fragments take their own time around it.
cues.evidence: Durand pp. 17–20 show the persistent B♭ figure, distributed between staves. The opening’s B♭ is a score fact, not a pitch identification derived from the audio model.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Two kinds of time
cues.text: Separate the regular bell from the slower changes of harmony. The repeated attacks measure time; the surrounding lines can seem suspended because they do not need to move with each attack.
cues.evidence: The repeated B♭ and independent chordal rhythms are visible throughout the score. This is a listening task for the movement, not a precisely timed change at 0:36.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: What makes the sound?
cues.text: Bertrand’s poem keeps asking what can be heard: an insect, a fly, a beetle, a spider? Its last sentence identifies a distant town bell and a hanged body reddened by the setting sun. The title means “The Gallows”.
cues.evidence: Original French poem, printed before the movement in the Durand edition: https://fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Gaspard_de_la_nuit_(%C3%A9d._1895)/Le_Gibet

cues.title: The score refuses haste
cues.text: Ravel writes “without hurrying or slowing to the end” and asks for the soft pedal throughout. Expression must come largely from balance, harmonic colour and register, rather than from treating each phrase as a fresh dramatic acceleration.
cues.evidence: Durand p. 17: Très lent; Sans presser ni ralentir jusqu’à la fin; Sourdine durant toute la pièce. These are printed instructions, not a measurement of this pianist’s compliance.

cues.title: Chords change the bell
cues.text: The surrounding piano sound gains weight in this region, but the recurring pitch remains the reference point. Listen for how a fixed note can seem to change character when its neighbouring notes change.
cues.evidence: The strongest measured boundary is at 2:28. Relative level reaches −10.4 dB at 2:30, above the opening’s lower-level windows. The score supplies the continuing bell; analysis alone does not identify the chords.

cues.title: Hear through the chord
cues.text: When the texture fills out, try to retain the repeated note inside it rather than listening only to the upper line. Ravel often writes across three staves so that one pair of hands can keep several layers distinct.
cues.evidence: Durand pp. 18–20 repeatedly use three staves to separate simultaneous piano layers. The cue does not assert a new entrance or a particular chord at 3:00.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The middle distance clears
cues.text: A retreat leaves the sound more exposed around this point. The recurring bell need not become louder to attract attention: reducing the weight around it can bring it forward.
cues.evidence: The report falls from −11.2 dB at 3:10 to −27.2 at 3:35, with a strong boundary at 3:32. Onsets are sparse at 3:25. The persistent note is established by the score.

cues.title: Quiet is not empty
cues.text: Listen for notes continuing to resonate after each attack. The soft-pedal instruction and the long values ask for a subdued but layered sound; a quiet passage can still contain several different rates of movement.
cues.evidence: Score-wide listening invitation grounded in the long chord values, repeated bell and soft-pedal instruction. No pedal change or acoustic effect has been measured at 4:12.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: One score, separate performances
cues.text: This is not the same recording session as the two surrounding movements. OE1FEU identifies the instrument as a Bechstein D 282 in Vienna’s Kaisersaal and dates the recording 3 April 2020; Makarevych’s two movements are dated 2014.
cues.evidence: Selected Commons source description identifies the instrument, place, author and date: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Maurice_Ravel-_Gaspard_de_la_Nuit-_II_Le_Gibet.flac. The other two selected sources explicitly give their performer and performance date.

cues.title: Weight without a new pulse
cues.text: The later span has gained weight again. Compare this with the exposed middle passage: the bell’s repetition stays recognisable while thicker sonorities renew the pressure around it.
cues.evidence: Following the change at 4:36, level rises to −10.9 dB at 4:40 and again at 5:30, versus −27.2 at 3:35. The unchanged recurring pitch is score evidence, not a tempo estimate.

cues.title: No release into daylight
cues.text: The closing page strips the texture back towards the bell and its supporting chords. There is no quick finale inside this movement: the pace remains slow as the layers lose their weight.
cues.evidence: Durand p. 20 returns to sparse bell-and-chord writing and closes ppp. The report declines broadly after 5:45 and again after 6:40; this is an approximate closing region.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The last resonances
cues.text: Keep listening after the final phrase has begun to withdraw. The bell has made repeated attacks seem almost permanent; the remaining resonance lets you hear the difference between stopping an attack and extinguishing its sound.
cues.evidence: The report falls from −19.0 dB at 6:40 to −47.7 at 7:00. This concerns the recorded decay, not an assertion about an exact final note or pedal release.

transitions.title: Keep the bell inside the change
transitions.how: Ravel changes the surrounding chords and spacing while retaining the recurring B♭. The fixed pitch links otherwise shifting colours: it is not a conventional dominant pedal that promises a single resolution. Independent melodic fragments and fuller sonorities enlarge the piano texture without replacing its basic pulse.
transitions.evidence: Durand pp. 18–19 retain the bell through varied chordal writing. The strong 2:28 boundary and higher relative levels at 2:15–2:30 provide the approximate anchor; no specific modulation is asserted.

transitions.title: Let the surrounding sound recede
transitions.how: The recurring note connects the fuller passage to a much lighter one. As the chordal weight recedes, attacks and the spaces around them become easier to separate. Ravel does not need a new tune or a faster tempo to create the contrast: removing some of the sound changes the apparent distance of what remains.
transitions.evidence: The 3:32 measured boundary lies within the 3:10–3:35 level decline, with sparse onsets around 3:25. The continuous bell is confirmed by Durand pp. 18–19.

transitions.title: Rebuild around the same note
transitions.how: After the lighter span, the surrounding harmonic layers gain weight again. The repeated B♭ supplies continuity while the chords renew the tension; the listener can compare changing vertical combinations against one fixed sound. This is a textural rebuilding, not a new movement or an escape from the slow pulse.
transitions.evidence: A measured boundary at 4:36 precedes the rise to −10.9 dB at 4:40. The score preserves the recurring B♭ throughout; the timing does not identify a particular chord.

transitions.title: Withdraw the layers, retain the bell
transitions.how: The final page returns to more widely spaced bell-and-chord writing and reduces the dynamic to ppp. The repeated note continues to connect the thinning layers. Ravel closes by withdrawing their weight, not by speeding into a cadential flourish: the piano’s remaining resonance becomes part of the ending.
transitions.evidence: Durand p. 20. The report declines from −12.2 dB at 5:45 to −24.5 at 6:20, with a further late decay after 6:40. The boundary is an approximate closing span, not a note-level alignment.

composer.background:
Ravel was born in Ciboure, across the harbour from Saint-Jean-de-Luz, to Marie Delouart, a Basque woman who had lived in Madrid, and Pierre-Joseph Ravel, a Swiss-born engineer. The family moved to Paris when Maurice was three months old. His father encouraged music as well as an interest in machinery; his mother’s songs gave him an early acquaintance with Spanish idioms. Basque ancestry and Spanish musical theatre remained distinct resources: the uneven pulse of the Piano Trio differs from the habanera of the Rapsodie espagnole. He returned to the Basque coast for holidays and composition, but received his musical education in Paris.

He entered the Conservatoire in 1889, initially as a pianist, and studied with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot. Failure to win the required prizes cost him his place in 1895. Readmitted in 1897 to Fauré’s composition class, he also learnt counterpoint from André Gedalge. Fauré encouraged the individual ear without relaxing the demands of construction; Gedalge supplied the discipline behind the fugues and independent inner parts. Ravel did not become a virtuoso pianist. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, introduced much of the difficult piano music, including Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit.
composer.epithet: An engineer of instrumental colour who made a piano imitate water, an orchestra imitate a machine, and old dances carry the names of the dead.
